articles.body:
Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning.

New open-source software could make AI-enhanced weather forecasting more affordable.

Researchers with the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make more accurate weather forecasts two to six weeks in advance — allowing farmers and emergency responders to plan ahead with greater certainty. The findings were published today in the journal Nature, and the tool is now open-source software.

Microsoft joins Google, Nvidia, and other companies developing AI tools for weather forecasting. Instead of creating a new standalone weather model, Microsoft’s latest research in this realm uses machine learning to correct bias in existing models. It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI, the researchers hope.

It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI

While physics-based modeling is a resource-intensive endeavor running on supercomputers and generative AI depends on powerful GPUs, Microsoft Research New England senior principal researcher Lester Mackey says the new tool can run just on CPUs. “I have a lot of hope both for the increased resource efficiency of weather forecasting and the extended reliability of forecasts, especially for extreme weather,” Mackey tells The Verge.

Physics-based and AI-based models run into similar problems when they start predicting the weather two weeks or more in advance. Traditional models attempt to simulate the complex physics of Earth’s atmosphere, while AI models look for patterns in historical data to make forecasts. In both approaches, models rely on approximations to fill data gaps, whether from regions with sparse weather stations or complex atmospheric phenomena that scientists are still working to understand. The ways in which these models make up for those gaps in data can become a type of systematic bias. The resulting errors compound when making forecasts further ahead in time, making these predictions less precise.

Microsoft calls its method Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC). The tool uses machine learning to identify systematic bias in a model and make corrections. One example Mackey gives is to correct for changes in climate. Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels are heating up the planet, but a weather model might make predictions based on historical records that can bias it toward colder temperatures than the world is actually experiencing today.

The researchers found that PBC improved the accuracy of a leading physics-based weather model by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for 98 percent of precipitation and 92 percent of temperature targets. The machine learning framework also doubled the accuracy of ECMWF’s new AI forecasting system in the study’s analysis. Before the paper was published, the ECMWF had already awarded the authors’ research on PBC in its AI Weather Quest competition.

The new paper on PBC published by researchers at Microsoft, MIT, ECMWF, and other institutions “is a good example of new ideas being developed for the benefit and consideration of the community,” Matthew Chantry, ECMWF’s strategic lead for machine learning, said in an emailed comment to The Verge.

“As always, turning ideas into reality [in] an operational process is a most challenging step,” Chantry added.

The amount of compute and infrastructure needed for weather forecasting has often left technological advances out of reach for many agencies in economically developing countries. The paper’s authors, however, think PBC can be different. “One of the things that’s really exciting to me about models like PBC is how lightweight they are, how easy to train, that scientists without huge pools of resources can work on trying to configure [these] models and make them perform better in specific localities,” says Genevieve Flaspohler, one of the authors of the paper.

Flaspohler worked on PBC as an intern at Microsoft with Mackey, and now she’s the executive director of the nonprofit Rhiza Research, which is working with the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority — with funding from the Gates Foundation — to see whether AI can help get more accurate early warnings out to people. PBC is one of the methods they’re testing ahead of what’s expected to be a more extreme rainy season during a record-breaking El Niño.

articles.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
articles.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.
articles.preview: A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications". As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings. But, here's we do know so far.
articles.body:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

But, here's we do know so far.

Help from a chatbot

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

Hiding in plain toilet paper

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?

Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.

Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

articles.body:
Floqer is an autonomous customer knowledge platform that provides business-to-business sales and marketing teams with an AI-powered database designed to continuously collect, organize, and update the information used to understand their customers.

Floqer is pitching Wednesday on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The startup told TechCrunch ahead of the presentation that it plans to open-source the technology behind its autonomous customer knowledge database. It’s targeting early 2027 for the release, pending security reviews.

Floqer also says it has surpassed $1.2 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), and that its overall revenue has grown roughly tenfold over the past year.

The startup was founded by Shivam Mahajan, the CEO, and Zaaheda Islam, who met at university. Before Floqer, Mahajan worked as a software engineer at Kyndryl, and Islam worked as a senior data scientist at Axis Capital.

Floqer’s first product looked nothing like its current one. “We started with a Chrome extension, which is called ‘Super Chat,’” Mahajan told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this month. “Anybody can go and log in with their ChatGPT account and then understand [information] and take notes.”

The founders soon noticed that enterprise companies were using the extension to clean up data in their customer relationship management (CRM) systems. Conversations with those companies showed that keeping CRM data clean was mostly manual work, with few established processes for keeping customer records up to date.

“When we spoke with them, they told us that it’s super manual for them to clean their CRM data, and there were no established processes around that,” Mahajan said. “So that was insightful for us, and then we pivoted from there to build Floqer.”

The problem Floqer is trying to solve is familiar to anyone who has worked in sales or revenue operations. Finding potential customers takes hours of searching Google, LinkedIn, company websites, job boards, and other sources to identify companies that fit a particular profile, then tracking down the right people and their contact information.

Floqer aims to automate much of that research. Users can describe what they are looking for, and its AI agents search across different sources to build lists of relevant companies and contacts.

The company says its system can enrich accounts, or add detail about the companies a sales team is targeting, using more than 100 third-party data sources. When it needs a verified email address or phone number, Floqer uses a “waterfall” approach, checking one data provider after another until it finds usable information.

The system also continuously monitors the web for changes. If a prospect changes jobs, gets promoted, or works at a company that raises new funding, those updates can be reflected in the user’s customer records.

Floqer describes the technology as a fleet of AI agents that continuously research companies, people, and customer interactions, so team members don’t have to perform that work manually. According to the company, customers have reported cutting prospecting time by as much as 70%.

“Our autonomous customer knowledge database is only available to a limited audience, mostly due to how much demand our team can actually serve properly,” Mahajan said. “But open-sourcing it will help us fix that.”

The decision comes partly in response to customer demand. Mahajan said some companies want to host their own data rather than keep it inside a vendor’s proprietary platform. Others want to modify the technology or build on top of it.

“Our mission is to really enable every team to build their central source of growth,” Mahajan said.

Before releasing the database publicly, Floqer is conducting security reviews because the database can contain sensitive customer information and large companies already use it.

Floqer was founded in 2024 and has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding, with participation from investors such as Perplexity’s F7 Fund, N49P, Tidal Venture Partners, and Perplexity co-founder Denis Yarats. It says it now has eight employees and more than 1,000 customers, including Perplexity, Wise, and AngelList.

United States federal agents have arrested a Saudi national and charged him with planting a hidden audio recording device in a conference room at the California offices of OpenAI, where he was working as an engineer.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had been working at the AI company since July 2025, the US Department of Justice said in a statement on Tuesday.

OpenAI discovered the device plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

Following the discovery, the company placed a camera in the room, which captured Alfozan entering last week and checking behind the television where the listening device had been installed, the FBI alleges.

The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete for the best talent and technology with the potential to alter regional economic and strategic dynamics.

Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan and what is he charged with?

Alfozan has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020.

According to a LinkedIn profile in his name, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said.

Before he joined OpenAI, he was a venture partner at Raed Ventures, headquartered in Riyadh in Saudi Arabia, which invested “in seed and early-stage startups in Saudi Arabia and MENA”.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the details mentioned in this LinkedIn profile.

Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday on a charge of “using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications”.

It was not immediately clear if he has legal representation. He is expected to return to court on October 19.

If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release.

What happened at OpenAI?

The FBI says a thumb-sized device with a microphone, and which could connect to a camera, had been concealed in toilet paper and placed behind a television set in the conference room. It was installed around September 28, the FBI said. Its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar device in Alfozan’s personal bag.

In a post on X, OpenAI said it had evidence that the employee intended to place other listening devices throughout sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the company said.

The FBI complaint also alleges that Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, despite not having the authority to access these spaces or participate in meetings there.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Hasn’t OpenAI been accused of helping to spy on civilians?

In an X post by OpenAI explaining how its own systems were used to trap Alfozan, the company said: “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.”

But AI technology is used not only to catch spying, but conversely, to engage in it as well.

In February 2025, an investigation by The Associated Press found that US tech giants had enabled Israel to track and kill people in Gaza and Lebanon through AI and computing services. The AP reported that the Israeli military had bought advanced AI tools from tech companies including OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, through Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform, to assist with surveillance.

OpenAI denies having a relationship with the Israeli military.

But OpenAI also faced criticism when it signed a deal with the US Department of Defense in February this year to supply its technology to the US military for use in classified settings, including intelligence gathering. OpenAI’s competitor, Anthropic, refused to sign the same deal unless the Pentagon barred mass surveillance of Americans.

There have been several incidents in which OpenAI models have gone “rogue” by independently breaking out of a testing environment and then hacking into other organisations and even government sites, leading to calls for stronger regulations against unchecked AI surveillance.

articles.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
articles.summary: Max Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, detailed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how his company's work with PRIMA is part of its path toward a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
articles.preview: Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI). “The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said.
articles.body:
Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).

“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”

Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.

While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.

Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.

“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”

The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.

To use the device, patients undergo an hourlong procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.

“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where … it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”

He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”

When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.

As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.

The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors.

“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”

Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said, it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.

“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.

articles.title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device in OpenAI office
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
articles.preview: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
articles.body:
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.

Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.

According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.

Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.

On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.

OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".

According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.

Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customising, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.

He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customis[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.

That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.

Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.

If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000).

articles.title: È stata pubblicata una versione gratuita della suite di Adobe fatta con l’AI
articles.summary: E poi anche dei software di Office, sempre usando Claude, apparentemente in poco tempo e con poco sforzo

articles.body:
E poi anche dei software di Office, sempre usando Claude, apparentemente in poco tempo e con poco sforzo

- Condividi

- X

La pubblicazione di versioni alternative e gratuite dei software di fotoritocco, montaggio video ed elaborazione grafica della suite di Adobe, come Photoshop e Premiere, ha attirato molte attenzioni e suscitato varie discussioni negli ultimi giorni, principalmente perché sono state realizzate in breve tempo e con apparente facilità grazie all’intelligenza artificiale. L’ingegnere che le ha pubblicate ha usato uno degli ultimi modelli di Claude, l’AI di Anthropic, e ha realizzato le copie dei programmi, del tutto simili agli originali, in circa una settimana. Poi ha fatto lo stesso coi programmi del pacchetto Office di Microsoft.

Gli abbonamenti per usare i software di Adobe sono notoriamente costosi, nell’ordine di decine di euro al mese, e sono usati da milioni di professionisti nel mondo. La legalità dell’operazione dell’ingegnere statunitense Brandon Thomas, che ha raccolto i programmi replicati in una suite che ha chiamato ArtCraft, è ancora molto incerta. Le prestazioni non sono al livello degli originali e sono stati segnalati vari bug e malfunzionamenti.

Ma è comunque una notizia piuttosto sorprendente e che ha confermato quanto sia diventato relativamente facile e rapido realizzare software complessi con l’AI, rinnovando le discussioni su quale sia il futuro dei modelli aziendali SaaS, Software as a Service, per cui le aziende fornitrici di software vendono i loro servizi tramite abbonamenti.

Adobe non ha ancora commentato. Non è un’azienda particolarmente amata: i suoi prodotti sono considerati di gran lunga i migliori sul mercato e sono lo standard per i professionisti, ma da anni è accusata dai suoi utenti di nascondere i costi di recesso degli abbonamenti. Nel 2024 il dipartimento di Giustizia statunitense l’ha citata in giudizio per la presunta violazione di una legge che impone alle aziende di essere trasparenti sui costi e di garantire disdette semplici, senza penali nascoste. Nel marzo del 2026 Adobe ha accettato di pagare 150 milioni di dollari, tra multe e crediti restituiti ai clienti, e si è impegnata ad adeguare i propri metodi di disdetta alla legge.

Thomas ha presentato ArtCraft definendolo un progetto in cui nessuno avrebbe dovuto più pagare delle penali per le cancellazioni e ha detto che lui stesso si è ritrovato più volte a dover pagare i costi di recesso dagli abbonamenti di Adobe.

ArtCraft è stata sviluppata attraverso il linguaggio di programmazione Rust e l’utilizzo di Opus 5.5, un modello premium di Claude rilasciato il 22 settembre. Thomas e il suo team hanno sfruttato gli agenti, cioè modelli di AI più potenti dei comuni chatbot, perché i software fossero programmati in buona parte autonomamente. Hanno avuto comunque un ruolo più attivo di quello che si intende normalmente per vibecoding, quando lo sviluppatore non scrive direttamente il codice ma dialoga con il modello in linguaggio naturale, come quando utilizza un chatbot per attività quotidiane.

ArtCraft è una suite open source, ovvero un insieme di programmi con un codice sorgente pubblico e liberamente accessibile: chiunque può scaricarlo, utilizzarlo o modificarlo. Nella suite sono disponibili applicazioni che replicano Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator e gli altri programmi di Adobe per la gestione di foto e di effetti visivi, l’impaginazione e la modifica di file PDF. L’interfaccia dei programmi replicati riproduce fedelmente quella degli originali: le impostazioni, gli strumenti e le scorciatoie da tastiera si trovano esattamente negli stessi posti e fanno le stesse cose. Questa somiglianza così plateale potrebbe esporre Thomas e il suo team a cause legali per violazione di brevetti e concorrenza sleale. Il trade dress, ovvero l’aspetto con cui un prodotto si presenta sul mercato e viene riconosciuto dai consumatori, è infatti tutelato da leggi specifiche in diversi paesi.

ArtCraft è ancora in uno stadio early alpha, un termine che nell’ambito informatico indica una versione embrionale di un software. Il giornalista Mike Pearl, del sito web specializzato Gizmodo, ha provato PhotoCraft, il programma che replica Photoshop, e ha riscontrato malfunzionamenti in alcune funzioni base. Nella sezione Issues di GitHub, dove vengono segnalati i malfunzionamenti dei software, alcuni utenti hanno poi evidenziato crash su diversi sistemi operativi. Gli stessi piani di sviluppo pubblicati dal team di Thomas hanno assegnato ai sette programmi replicati una percentuale di “sviluppo per il lavoro reale” compresa solo tra il 45 e il 61 per cento.

Molte delle segnalazioni su GitHub riguardano i salvataggi su PhotoCraft. Molti file vengono danneggiati, le immagini rovinate e, in alcuni casi, gli utenti non riescono a salvare i loro lavori. PhotoCraft può risultare quindi utile per lavorare su copie di backup, mentre può essere rischioso per lavori importanti o con scadenze imminenti. Inoltre, negli ultimi giorni sono stati creati moltissimi siti non ufficiali che replicano a loro volta la suite di ArtCraft e che possono essere rischiosi per chi li scarica sul proprio computer.

Thomas ha sostenuto che la suite è stata creata attraverso un’operazione clean-room, una procedura di sviluppo che prevede la riscrittura da zero del codice a partire dalla sola osservazione del programma e da documentazioni pubbliche, senza mai accedere al codice sorgente originale.

Questo tipo di processo si inserisce nell’ambito del reverse engineering (o ingegneria inversa), che prevede l’analisi di un software, ma anche di oggetti fisici come i chip, per comprenderne il funzionamento e ricostruirlo. Tuttavia, per far sì che una procedura possa essere definita clean-room il lavoro deve essere svolto da due team distinti: uno che studia il programma originale e redige istruzioni e un altro che scrive il codice senza aver visto il software. Nel caso di ArtCraft, invece, un solo team ha svolto entrambe le mansioni utilizzando un modello AI addestrato su enormi quantità di dati e di codice presi dal web.

articles.title: Tehran municipality accused of ‘overstep’ after launching welfare projects
articles.summary: Tehran's new municipal welfare projects face intense criticism over funding sources, transparency, and inflation claims.
articles.preview: Tehran’s municipality has launched new welfare initiatives to combat inflation, drawing intense scrutiny over funding sources, institutional overlap, and transparency. articles.body:
Tehran’s municipality has launched new welfare initiatives to combat inflation, drawing intense scrutiny over funding sources, institutional overlap, and transparency.

Tehran municipality has launched a series of welfare initiatives to help residents cope with soaring living costs, but the measures have raised questions about their financing and effectiveness, as well as whether the local authority is taking on responsibilities better handled by Iran’s national government.

The local authority has launched four projects it says are aimed at protecting citizens, including a housing project, freezes on the prices of 12 basic goods, and a maternity package.

Questions have been raised about how they will be funded and whether the municipality is overstepping its traditional functions.

In Iran, municipalities are responsible for local services and urban management, while the national government oversees broader economic policy, including efforts to control inflation.

Iranian law does give municipalities some responsibilites beyond conventional urban services, but Article 55 of Iran’s Municipal Law does call for municipalities to provide for public food markets, make certain essential goods more affordable, and provide social welfare facilities and low-cost housing.

The dispute is therefore less about whether Tehran municipality can provide the services, and more about their scale and financing.

The municipality’s price-freezing initiative, dubbed the “Zero Inflation” project, has been the most controversial. It comes as year-on-year inflation reached nearly 90 percent last month, while annual food inflation hit 108.8 percent.

Doubts have been raised about how the project will be funded and its effectiveness. Others believe that the measures could fuel inequality between the capital and other cities.

They are viewed as steps to address the huge economic challenges faced by Tehran residents, worsened since the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28.

Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani said the municipality had recently guaranteed prices ranging between 5 percent and 50 percent below market rates for the next six months.

Yousef Akandeh, a political activist, told Al Jazeera that freezing the prices of some goods or providing free services will not reduce inflation to zero alone.

“Even if we assume that the Tehran municipality succeeded in stabilising the prices of 12 basic goods, what about the rise in rents, medicines, transportation prices, and the rest of living expenses,” Akandeh asked.

Real steps to tackle inflation, Akandeh said, would have to begin with controlling liquidity growth and monetary discipline, which he said are nearly impossible amid the ongoing war.

The municipality has also introduced a maternity support programme offering mothers of children born this year monthly credits worth up to 40 million rials ($15) for two years for each newborn.

Akandeh raised the issue of institutional overlap, noting that a similar national scheme already exists.

“The government implements a similar package and provides monthly financial amounts for all newborns across the country and not just in Tehran, and if the municipality’s package is independent of it, the Tehrani family may benefit from the national and municipal programme simultaneously,” Akandeh said.

Receiving support from both programmes would not, in itself, indicate wrongdoing. But critics are instead raising the question of whether it is an appropriate use of Tehran’s municipal resources, particularly when the city faces competing spending demands.

Amir Dabiri Mehr, a former adviser in the Tehran municipality, told Al Jazeera that although supporting the homeless falls under the municipality’s social responsibilities, the problem lies in a lack of transparency. The municipality is funded by taxes and building density licences.

“The people have the right to know what the municipality spends within the framework of its original tasks, and in tasks it has chosen for itself, and where it gets its resources from?” Dabiri Mehr said.

The municipality-affiliated Hamshahri newspaper said that the “Zero Inflation” project is not funded by municipal budget subsidies, but through direct purchases from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in council-run stores.

The biggest crisis facing Tehran’s residents is housing, which is the national government’s responsibility, Mehr said. Food and living expenses are the national government’s responsibility.

“If the goal is to solve the people’s problems, it seems that the biggest problem facing the residents of Tehran today is the housing crisis, and this dilemma cannot be solved by building an apartment building consisting of a few residential units,” he said.

Al Jazeera attempted to contact the Tehran municipality for comment but received no response.

Tehran Mayor Zakani has, however, defended the financing arrangements, telling a local newspaper, Hamshahri, that the Zero Inflation initiative would not rely on direct subsidies from the municipal budget, but instead on purchasing goods directly from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in city-run stores.

Zakani also said that the programme would draw on municipal resources, bank financing, and partnerships.

Retired Americans will see a $75 boost in monthly cheques as benefits rise amid widespread inflation challenges.

United States Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent beginning in 2027, marking one of the largest cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) of the decade.

On Wednesday, the Social Security Administration announced the hike after the Bureau of Labor Statistics published the Consumer Price Index for September. The alteration represents a four-year high, boosting average monthly cheques by $75 for older adults and people with disabilities.

The benefit bump will roll out in January for 72 million Social Security recipients, and on December 31, for nearly 73 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) beneficiaries.

Starting in 2027, the maximum limit for a taxable wage base, or income cap, is slated to increase to $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026.

The social security programme is the largest federal social insurance framework in the country. The entitlement programme provides financial support for older adults and disabled people, as well as benefits for survivors of families of workers who have passed away. Funded through dedicated payroll taxes, it serves primarily as a federal pension system that replaces a portion of an individual’s pre-retirement income upon leaving the workforce.

The agency bases the annual increase, closely watched by retirees and others receiving benefits, on the average of the annual increase in the CPI for urban wage earners and clerical workers, also known as the CPI-W index. That index rose 3.9 percent in September and averaged about 3.6 percent for the three months of July, August and September. For 2026, the increase was 2.8 percent.

The announcement comes as high US inflation continues to remain a persistent economic headwind, fuelled primarily by energy shocks from the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have caused global energy market turmoil that has sent crude oil prices above $100 a barrel.

More recently, refined petroleum products like diesel fuel have climbed to record highs and have contributed to a widening of inflationary pressures.

Most older adults in the US believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5 percent COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.

articles.body:
Economists divided on Fed rate hike as inflation creates uncertainty in run-up to US midterm elections in a tense market.

United States consumer prices jumped in September in the final inflation report before the midterm elections, increasing chances of an interest rate hike later this month.

Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6 percent, according to the Consumer Price Index report released by the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.

- list 2 of 4Gold falls amid rising oil prices and higher US dollar

- list 3 of 4Indian firm building $15bn Trump-announced steel mill has deep Russia ties

- list 4 of 4Trump says Houthis trying to increase oil prices before US elections

Petrol prices led the surge as tensions between the US and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, weighed on global energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the CPI monthly increase, according to the BLS. They were up 34.2 percent from the same time a year ago.

“The directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains, driving up the prices of food and fuel,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, an economic think tank, said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.

Petrol prices have continued to climb. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.33 ($1.14 per litre), compared with $4.31 a month ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. Diesel prices are higher, at $6.29 per gallon (1.66 per litre), compared with $6.23 a month ago.

In a post on X, Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said, “2026 has now seen more days with average gas prices over $4/gal than any year before: 158 days.”

Shelter costs also jumped 0.4 percent from the previous month, following a 0.3 percent increase in August. Food costs were a bright spot in the report, remaining unchanged overall.

Food away from home, including restaurant meals, rose 0.2 percent, but that increase was offset by a 0.1 percent decline in food-at-home prices, which track grocery costs.

At the grocery store, poultry prices jumped 0.7 percent, fruit and vegetable prices rose 0.5 percent, and juice prices increased 1.1 percent. However, milk prices dropped 2.1 percent and beef prices fell 0.9 percent.

Amid heavy investment in AI infrastructure, prices for computer software and accessories have jumped 28 percent from the same time last year.

“The AI boom is playing a huge part, and we have all read about the hundreds of billions being poured into data centers, AI firms, and models,” Rami Cassis, principal of Parabellum Investment, said in comments provided to Al Jazeera.

Fed pressures

The inflation data comes days before the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this month. Last month, the US central bank raised rates by 25 basis points, bringing the target range to 3.75–4.00 percent, the first hike in three years.

Economists are divided over whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. According to CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, there is a 52.9 percent chance that rates will remain in the 3.75–4.00 percent range, while a 47.1 percent chance of a quarter of a percentage point hike that would bring them to 4.00–4.25 percent.

The inflation data puts pressure on Republicans before the midterm elections on November 3. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that about 78 percent of Americans blamed US President Donald Trump’s policies for price increases.

US markets trended downward following the inflation report. The Nasdaq fell 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.6 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was roughly flat in midday trading.

articles.title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
articles.summary: The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
articles.preview: US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August. Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US. What is inflation?
articles.body:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.

Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.

What is inflation?

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

What causes inflation?

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

What is the current rate of inflation?

Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.

Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.

In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.

Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.

Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.

At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

Will the inflation hike change Social Security payments?

Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost of living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72m people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

How have tariffs affected inflation?

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

Has inflation been worse lately?

While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

Can inflation ever go down?

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

articles.title: Confindustria: 'Crescita fragile, Pil 2026 a +1%, poi cala'
articles.summary: L'energia prima vulnerabilità, crescita zero se media Brent sale a 126 dollari
articles.preview: "Nel 2026 il Pil cresce sopra le attese al +1%", stima il Centro studi di Confindustria con il rapporto di autunno sulle previsioni economiche. E avverte: è una "crescita fragile". "Nel 2027 il rallentamento si farà sentire": la crescita stimata per il prossimo anno si ferma al +0,6% per effetto "della debolezza della fase finale del 2026 e di un recupero solo moderato a inizio anno". "Energia, inflazione e tassi frenano la crescita".
articles.body:
"Nel 2026 il Pil cresce sopra le attese al +1%", stima il Centro studi di Confindustria con il rapporto di autunno sulle previsioni economiche. E avverte: è una "crescita fragile". "Nel 2027 il rallentamento si farà sentire": la crescita stimata per il prossimo anno si ferma al +0,6% per effetto "della debolezza della fase finale del 2026 e di un recupero solo moderato a inizio anno".

"Energia, inflazione e tassi frenano la crescita". Il costo dell'energia "resta la più importante vulnerabilità dell'economia italiana" tanto che "potrebbe annullare la crescita del Pil prevista" per il prossimo anno: gli economisti di Confindustria avvertono che sarà crescita zero nel caso di "un Brent a circa 126 dollari al barile in media annua".

In Italia resta una "crescita fragile tra shock internazionali e sfide per le imprese", rileva il centro studi di Confindustria. L'ipotesi alla base delle stime "è che dopo le elezioni di midterm negli Stati Uniti si trovi una soluzione alla guerra Usa-Iran": per gli economisti di viale dell'Astronomia la crisi dello Stretto di Hormuz "sarebbe sostenibile fino a maggio prossimo", se si va oltre "sarebbe difficile approvvigionarsi e salirebbero le quotazioni del petrolio a livelli mai visti prima". Per quest'anno la crescita attesa è rivista al rialzo grazie al "buon andamento dell'economia italiana nella prima metà dell'anno"; al "decisivo apporto del Pnrr (+0,5 punti percentuali di Pil)"; al "contenuto trasferimento dei rincari energetici agli altri beni e servizi". La crescita "poggia sui consumi (+1,1%, molto meglio quelli delle famiglie di quelli pubblici) e sugli investimenti (+3,3%), trainati nel complesso dalle costruzioni nonostante il calo della componente abitativa. Resta invece negativo l'apporto della domanda estera netta nonostante la crescita dell'export (+2,7% quello di beni, +3,8% quello di servizi)". La crescita 2027 "dovrebbe rallentare a un ritmo in linea con quello osservato nel 2025".

Peseranno "il prezzo del petrolio tornato a settembre sui livelli massimi"; "il prezzo del gas che ha raggiunto a settembre i livelli più alti dalla fine del 2022 ed è atteso rimanere così fino a fine anno"; "l'aumento del tasso di inflazione che, a settembre, ha toccato il suo massimo raggiungendo il 4,2% spinto dai rincari energetici e ridurrà il potere d'acquisto delle famiglie frenando i consumi nella parte finale dell'anno e poi anche all'inizio del 2027"; ed "i rialzi dei tassi di interesse. Il maggior costo del denaro frenerà consumi e investimenti". Pesa anche la fine del Pnrr che comporta "un rallentamento della spesa per investimenti, moderato dalle ampie risorse residuate che verranno spese dopo il 2026 (circa 47 miliardi, di cui 27 nel 2027, significativamente meno dei circa 42 miliardi spesi nel 2026)". Nel 2027 "la dinamica del Pil sarà ancora trainata dai consumi delle famiglie e dagli investimenti, che però rallenteranno significativamente: +0,5% e +0,8% rispettivamente. Le esportazioni nette torneranno a fornire un lieve apporto positivo, favorito dal miglioramento delle ragioni di scambio, ma l'export rallenterà (+1,5% i beni, +2,5% i servizi)". I "rischi dello scenario di previsione" del centro studi di viale dell'Astronomia "sono legati all'evolversi dei transiti delle navi per lo Stretto di Hormuz e più in generale alla guerra nel Golfo". "Un altro rischio dello scenario è legato alla volatilità sui mercati finanziari, causata proprio dalla tensione nel mercato mondiale del petrolio e del gas e dai suoi riflessi sulle quotazioni, sull'inflazione e, a cascata, sulle decisioni delle banche centrali relative ai tassi". Il rapporto registra anche che "in Europa negli ultimi giorni sono bruscamente saliti i rendimenti dei titoli sovrani, di più in Francia, ma anche in Italia, e maggiori acquisti di titoli tedeschi, con un allargamento degli spread. Se una tale tendenza proseguisse - avverte - porrebbe un freno alla crescita in tutto il Continente".

articles.title: Centro Studi Confindustria: stima Pil 2026 alzata a +1%, il 2027 resta a +0,6%
articles.summary: Pubblicato il Rapporto di previsione d’autunno del CsC: deficit-Pil al 2,9% quest’anno
articles.preview: Pubblicato il Rapporto di previsione d’autunno del CsC: deficit-Pil al 2,9% quest’anno Una crescita del pil per il 2026 all’1%, sopra le attese indicate a marzo. Un dato positivo dovuto al buon andamento dell’economia italiana nella prima metà dell’anno, al contributo del Pnrr, (+0,5 punti nel 2026, spingendo soprattutto gli investimenti), al contenuto trasferimento dei rincari energetici agli altri beni e servizi, al rincaro inferiore alle aspettative del prezzo del petrolio.
articles.body:
Pubblicato il Rapporto di previsione d’autunno del CsC: deficit-Pil al 2,9% quest’anno

Una crescita del pil per il 2026 all’1%, sopra le attese indicate a marzo. Un dato positivo dovuto al buon andamento dell’economia italiana nella prima metà dell’anno, al contributo del Pnrr, (+0,5 punti nel 2026, spingendo soprattutto gli investimenti), al contenuto trasferimento dei rincari energetici agli altri beni e servizi, al rincaro inferiore alle aspettative del prezzo del petrolio.

Crescita fragile, per le imprese la sfida degli shock internazionali

Ma è una «crescita fragile, tra shock internazionali e sfide per le imprese»: nel 2027 l’economia dovrebbe rallentare e la stima per il pil si ferma allo 0,6% per effetto della debolezza della fase finale del 2026 e di un recupero solo moderato a inizio anno. È lo scenario del Rapporto di previsione del Centro studi di Confindustria.

Energia, inflazione e tassi frenano lo sviluppo

Energia, inflazione e tassi frenano la crescita. L’ipotesi alla base dello scenario è che dopo le elezioni Usa di midterm si trovi una soluzione alla guerra tra Stati Uniti e Iran, come annunciato da Trump, e che da gennaio i transiti attraverso Hormuz riprendano con normalità.

Costo dell’energia ed Ets rischiano di annullare la crescita

Un fattore determinante, dal momento che l’energia resta «la principale vulnerabilità dell’economia italiana». Secondo il Centro studi con un Brent a circa 126 dollari al barile in media annua nel 2027, rispetto ai 75 dello scenario di base e ai 94 di quest’anno, «la crescita del pil prevista per il 2027 si potrebbe annullare». Lo stesso accadrebbe con il prezzo del petrolio in media a 115 dollari al barile e quello del gas a 89 euro mwh (invece dei 58 dello scenario base).

Nella manifattura italiana emissioni in calo del 43%

Energia e Ets sono «macigni» sulla competitività delle imprese, sostiene in Csc, che sull’Ets ha messo a punto un approfondimento: i benefici in termini di emissioni, nella manifattura, sono in gran parte dovuti alla chiusura delle imprese. Nella sola manifattura italiana sottoposta a Ets tra il 2005 e il 2025 le emissioni sono diminuite del 43%, ma nello stesso periodo sono stati chiusi 386 impianti, 19 all’anno.

articles.body:
Nasce una nuova società partecipata al 51% dal broker italiano. Obiettivo: raggiungere 10 milioni di dollari di fatturato entro il 2028

Cambiaso Risso, uno dei principali broker internazionali specializzati nei rischi marittimi e navali, entra nel mercato sudamericano attraverso una partnership con una società brasiliana, focalizzandosi sui settori marittimo, navale, portuale, offshore e oil & gas. L’azienda genovese ha avviato le proprie attività in Brasile attraverso una joint venture con la società brasiliana Korsa riscos & seguros; nasce quindi Cr Korsa Brasil.

La nuova società sarà partecipata al 51% da Cambiaso Risso e al 49% da Korsa. L’obiettivo è rafforzare la presenza del gruppo internazionale sul mercato brasiliano per espandersi sugli altri mercati dell’America Latina. Cr Korsa prevede di raggiungere un fatturato di 10 milioni di dollari annui, a partire dal 2028. Le aree di attività della società comprenderanno il trasporto marittimo, corpi nave e macchinari (hull & machinery), responsabilità civile, porti, costruzioni e riparazioni navali, operazioni offshore, oil & gas, energia, superyacht, merci e coperture P&i (protection & indemnity). Cr Korsa dedicherà, inoltre, particolare attenzione ai progetti di sviluppo delle infrastrutture marittime, portuali e offshore del Brasile.

Con sede a Rio de Janeiro, uno dei principali cluster marittimi del Paese, la nuova struttura servirà i mercati del Sudest, del Nord e del Nordest del Brasile, spiega una nota, «senza limitazioni legate alla dimensione dei clienti». James Theodoro, attuale ceo di Korsa riscos & seguros, assumerà il ruolo di ceo di Cr Korsa Brasil e guiderà le attività della nuova società.

«Oltre alla nostra consolidata leadership globale nel ramo hull e alla crescente presenza nel P&i - afferma Mauro Iguera, ceo del gruppo Cambiaso Risso - l’America Latina ci offre l’opportunità di sviluppare ulteriormente gli altri due pilastri della nostra strategia, energy/offshore e riassicurazione, in stretta collaborazione con i nostri uffici di Londra e della Scandinavia». Uno degli elementi distintivi della nuova operazione, aggiunge Iguera, sarà l’accesso ai mercati internazionali. Cambiaso Risso dispone, infatti, di una rete globale di specialisti dedicati al settore marittimo, compreso un team a Londra che supporterà lo sviluppo delle attività originate dal Brasile.

Mercato in espansione

Secondo alcune stime della nuova società, il mercato assicurativo brasiliano collegato ai settori marittimo, navale, portuale e offshore ha generato circa 2,5 miliardi di real brasiliani di premi, collocati nel 2025. Peraltro, l’offerta della nuova società andrà oltre la tradizionale attività e comprenderà brokeraggio assicurativo e riassicurativo; consulenza sui rischi; consulenza nella gestione dei sinistri, anche per aziende non clienti; servizi di risk management per clienti portuali, marittimi e oil & gas; gestione di programmi di welfare aziendale, con particolare attenzione a salute e qualità della vita.

articles.title: «Sull’IA un Piano e una Zes per favorire gli investimenti»
articles.summary: Un piano d’azione che metta a sistema il mondo della ricerca, gli incentivi e le infrastrutture
articles.preview: Un piano d’azione che metta a sistema il mondo della ricerca, gli incentivi e le infrastrutture «L’intelligenza artificiale è la più grande rivoluzione dell’età contemporanea. Ha riflessi sul lavoro, sulle aziende, sulla società, può far fare un salto di qualità molto rapido alle nostre imprese, specialmente le piccole. È una sfida che l’Italia deve vincere».
articles.body:
Un piano d’azione che metta a sistema il mondo della ricerca, gli incentivi e le infrastrutture

«L’intelligenza artificiale è la più grande rivoluzione dell’età contemporanea. Ha riflessi sul lavoro, sulle aziende, sulla società, può far fare un salto di qualità molto rapido alle nostre imprese, specialmente le piccole. È una sfida che l’Italia deve vincere». Maria Anghileri, presidente dei Giovani Imprenditori di Confindustria, riprende un dato citato dal governatore della Banca d’Italia: con un’adozione rapida e diffusa dell’intelligenza artificiale la produttività del lavoro potrebbe aumentare di oltre un punto percentuale all’anno. «Una percentuale determinante per un Paese come l’Italia che deve tornare a crescere». L’IA sarà al centro del convegno di Capri che si apre venerdì: “StrategIA. Il futuro è un’impresa umana”. «Questa tecnologia può modificare le nostre capacità, ma resta una scelta umana come usarle. Non si tratta di scegliere tra uomo e macchina, è più importante decidere cosa vogliamo affidarle, unendo intelligenza artificiale e intelligenza imprenditoriale».

Il nostro Paese è indietro nella digitalizzazione e quindi nell’applicazione dell’intelligenza artificiale. Come possiamo rapidamente recuperare terreno?

La realtà italiana è che le piccole imprese fanno fatica ad applicare l’IA per motivi di costo e formazione. L’Italia si è dotata di una Strategia per l’Intelligenza artificiale che ora va implementata con azioni concrete e mirate. La nostra proposta è un “AI Adoption Act”, un piano d’azione che metta a sistema il mondo della ricerca, gli incentivi e le infrastrutture da attuare con una cabina di regia che coordini gli interventi per l’adozione e lo sviluppo dell’IA in Italia. Occorre creare un ecosistema per supportare le imprese che adottano l’intelligenza artificiale, lo vediamo nel road show che stiamo facendo come Giovani Imprenditori insieme ad Alberto Tripi, special advisor di Confindustria per l’IA. Esistono molti casi di eccellenza, manca il coordinamento.

È solo un problema di costi?

No, servono prima di tutto le competenze, e quindi occorre investire su scuole, università e formazione continua dei lavoratori. E poi lavorare sui processi aziendali e investire nella digitalizzazione. Spesso le piccole imprese non hanno risorse sufficienti per una adozione profonda dell’IA che porti a una vera trasformazione aziendale. È un percorso molto complicato, ma necessario.

Come attivare gli investimenti che servono?

La nostra proposta, che lanceremo a Capri, è la creazione di Zes-IA per convogliare investimenti pubblici e privati nell’intelligenza artificiale, anche attraverso l’uso di strumenti finanziari specifici per start up e imprese innovative. Investimenti da realizzare attraverso un canale semplificato riprendendo il modello della Zes unica che ha funzionato bene al Sud.
